questions.problem:
What is the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ for $x<0$ with $f(x)=\frac{|8x-7|}{-5x+2}?$

The horizontal asymptote is $y=$

{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
For large negative values of $x,$ we have $|8x-7|=-(8x-7).$ Consequently, for $x\to -\infty ,$ we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{|8x-7|}{-5x+2}={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(8x-7)}{-5x+2}.
$$

The horizontal asymptote for $x<0$ is $y={lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(8x-7)}{-5x+2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(\frac{8x}{x}-\frac{7}{x})}{(\frac{-5x}{x}+\frac{2}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(8-\frac{7}{x})}{(-5+\frac{2}{x})} \\  & =\frac{-(8-0)}{-5+0} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\frac{8}{5}.$

questions.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have ${S}_{1}=[0,2]$

- if $i=2,$ we have ${S}_{2}=[0,\frac{3}{2}]$

- if $i=3,$ we have ${S}_{3}=[0,\frac{4}{3}]$

and so on. 

Notice that as $i$ increases, 

- the left endpoint of the intervals is $0$ for all the sets,

- the right endpoint of the intervals approaches $1$ but never reaches it.

Moreover, all the intervals are contained in ${S}_{1}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}={S}_{1}=[0,2].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A  linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation. Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}48 \\ -6\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}48 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =6v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=6v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=6.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x),$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x).$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & ={e}^{|-x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={e}^{|x|}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)) \\  & =-{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x+p & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =-p.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $a=⟨-5,-3,1⟩$ and $b=⟨x,-2,-3⟩.$ Given that the projection of $a$ onto $b$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =-5\cdot x+(-3)\cdot (-2)+1\cdot (-3) \\  & =3-5x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 3-5x & =0 \\ -5x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $U={p,q,r,s,t,u}$ is the universal set and $S={q,s,t},$ then the complement of $S$ is
questions.worked_solution:
The complement of $S,$ denoted $\overset{―}{S},$ consists of every element in the universal set $U$ that is not in the set $S.$

The only elements of $U$ that are not in $S$ are $p,$ $r,$ and $u.$

Therefore, the complement of $S$ is

$$
\overset{―}{S}={p,r,u}.
$$

questions.problem: The third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!} \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡0=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(0) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡0=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =0+2\cdot x+0\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+(-8)\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =2x-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
